newsitem.title: FRANCE: French aides differ on possible corporate tax hike.
newsitem.headline: French aides differ on possible corporate tax hike.

text.p: France's Socialist-led government sent mixed signals on Wednesday on whether it planned to raise taxes on corporate profits to help cap the public deficit this year to qualify for a single European currency.

Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann told a news conference after the weekly cabinet meeting: "We are looking at the possibility of calling for an extra effort from companies and this would be made by companies which are profitable."
But Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said later after briefing parliament that no decisions had been taken on any new budget measures.
Trautmann's statement knocked French stocks, with the CAC-40 blue-chip index falling by more than two percent after rising earlier in the day.

Strauss-Kahn then sought to calm the markets and dampen speculation about possible tax hikes, which would be used to fund new spending measures announced by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and help meet the conditions for European monetary union (EMU).
"Nothing has been decided in any area," he told reporters in parliament when asked about the reported plan to raise corporate taxation.
A finance ministry source close to Strauss-Kahn added: "If you are asking, 'Is there today a plan concerning taxation of company profits?'...no such plan exists."

The source noted the government had pledged to shift the burden of taxation off labour costs and on to capital. But it did not want to increase the overall tax burden and wanted to maintain the competitiveness of French companies.
If the government were to change taxation on companies, it would have to be in that context, he said, adding: "We are not there yet. Today there is no proposal being studied."
He added that the new spending measures estimated to cost some 12 billion francs ($2 billion) this year would be offset by the freezing of an equivalent amount of other public spending.
Trautmann said the issue had not been discussed in cabinet, adding that any decision would have to take account of the results of an audit of public finances due on July 21.

Earlier, Socialist party leader Francois Hollande told Europe 1 radio: "If an extra effort is to be made, it will not be on households, it will not be the French people, it will be on those who have made the most profit in the last few years.
"The profitable company will pay."
Hollande said the French government aimed to meet its commitments made before the June 1 parliamentary election and to EU partners.
Trautmann said if there were new tax measures, these would be submitted to parliament in September.
Financial daily La Tribune said the government was looking at raising taxes to limit the deficit to around 3.3 percent of gross domestic product this year to prepare France for EMU.
A government source has said the deficit could otherwise be more than 3.4 or 3.5 percent of GDP this year -- above a level seen as acceptable for EMU entry to France's EU partners.

The satirical-investigative weekly Le Canard Enchaine said the government appeared keen to decide measures to reduce the deficit this year before publication of the audit, which it said could forecast the deficit at 3.6 or 3.7 percent of GDP.

It said finance ministry budget advisors were suggesting raising savings taxes to 25 percent from 20.9, increasing taxes on company capital gains to 33 percent from 19 percent and capping tax breaks on life assurance contracts.
La Tribune said the government would also look at other ways of increasing revenues, including a one-off charge of about 10 billion francs on state-owned savings banks Caisse d'Epargne.
A reduction of 0.3 percentage points in the deficit would represent some 24 billion francs. ($ = 5.897 French Francs)
